metadata.title: Got math attitude? (In)direct effects of student mathematics attitudes on intentions, behavioral engagement, and mathematics performance in the U.S. PISA

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses the U.S. PISA 2012 public-use dataset and relies on PISA’s complex survey design to support population generalization. For descriptive statistics and composite indicators, the authors used the final student weight function (WFSTUWT) in SPSS. For the SEM analyses, they used replicate weights via Mplus REPWEIGHT with WFSTR1–WFSTR80 to adjust standard errors for sampling variance. The SEM also incorporates the five mathematics plausible values simultaneously (TYPE = Imputation), producing averaged estimates across plausible values; the manuscript does not indicate any omission of weights for the main inferential models.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The paper does not report a conventional missing-data handling label for the background questionnaire items in the way the schema expects (e.g., listwise deletion vs multiple imputation). Instead, it states that because the rotated questionnaire design leads to missingness considered MCAR, the authors did not use multiple imputation and estimated the SEM using full information maximum likelihood (FIML) in Mplus with all available data. This is a missing-data strategy, but it is not mapped explicitly to the schema’s missing-data categories in the provided text, so the handling is treated as not_reported for strict extraction.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used the U.S. PISA 2012 public-use data file for 15-year-old students, with mathematics as the focal domain because it was the competency focus in 2012. The manuscript does not describe additional task- or grade-specific exclusions beyond the PISA rotated questionnaire structure; it reports that the dataset includes N = 4,978 participants and that missingness from the rotated design was treated as MCAR and handled via FIML in Mplus using all available data.

main_findings.performance_metrics: SEM (replicate-weighted) explained variance: R² = 0.211 (SE = 0.013), p < 0.001. Direct effects: Attitude → Intentions β = 0.420 (SE = 0.026, p < 0.001); Subjective norms → Intentions β = -0.083 (SE = 0.030, p < 0.05); Perceived behavioral control → Intentions β = 0.058 (SE = 0.039, p = 0.132).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2012 (U.S.) mathematics literacy the study leveraged Attitude towards mathematics, Subjective norms, and Perceived behavioral control (controlling for Gender, Race/ethnicity, and ESCS) to predict Mathematics intentions, finding that Attitude had a positive direct effect while Subjective norms had a small negative direct effect and Perceived behavioral control was not significant. This indicates that interventions should prioritize improving students’ mathematics attitudes and carefully manage social-pressure messages that may undermine intentions, though the cross-sectional design limits causal claims.

main_findings.performance_metrics: SEM explained variance: R² = 0.594 (SE = 0.022), p < 0.001. Direct effects: Perceived behavioral control → Behavior β = 0.719 (SE = 0.018, p < 0.001); Intentions → Behavior β = 0.064 (SE = 0.019, p < 0.05). Attitude → Behavior indirect (via intentions) β = 0.027 (SE = 0.009, p = 0.009).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2012 (U.S.) mathematics literacy the study leveraged Perceived behavioral control and Intentions (with Attitude and demographic/SES controls) to predict Behavioral engagement (mathematics work ethic), finding that Perceived behavioral control had a strong positive direct effect while Intentions had only a small positive direct effect. This indicates that strengthening self-efficacy and students’ sense of controllability may be more effective for improving day-to-day mathematics work habits than focusing solely on long-term intentions, though causality cannot be inferred.

main_findings.target_variable: Mathematics performance (PVs, averaged across five plausible values)
main_findings.performance_metrics: SEM explained variance: R² = 0.307 (SE = 0.013), p < 0.001. Direct effects: Behavior → Math performance β = 0.255 (SE = 0.016, p < 0.001). Indirect effects: Perceived behavioral control → Math performance via Behavior alone β = 0.184 (SE = 0.014, p < 0.001); Attitude → Math performance via Intentions & Behavior β = 0.006 (SE = 0.018, p = 0.009); Subjective norms → Math performance via Intentions & Behavior β = -0.001 (SE = 0.000, p = 0.010).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2012 (U.S.) mathematics literacy the study leveraged Mathematics work ethic and the TPB constructs (Attitude, Subjective norms, Perceived behavioral control) to predict Mathematics performance (plausible values), finding that Behavioral engagement had a positive direct effect and that Perceived behavioral control improved performance indirectly through Behavioral engagement. This indicates that policy and practice should target students’ mathematics work habits and self-efficacy/control beliefs to translate attitudes into achievement, while recognizing that the model is correlational and uses secondary cross-sectional data.

data.outcome_summary: This study analyzes the U.S. PISA 2012 mathematics literacy domain using a theory of planned behavior (TPB) structural model to examine (in)direct relations among mathematics attitudes, intentions, behavioral engagement (work ethic), and mathematics performance. The analytic sample includes N = 4,978 U.S. 15-year-olds, and the authors use PISA’s complex survey design with replicate weights (WFSTR1–WFSTR80) in Mplus. Mathematics performance is modeled using five plausible values, with the SEM estimating and averaging across plausible values (TYPE = Imputation). The model explains R² = 0.211 of intentions, R² = 0.594 of behavioral engagement, and R² = 0.307 of mathematics performance; key paths include Attitude → Intentions (β = 0.420) and Behavior → Performance (β = 0.255). Limitations include the absence of causal identification and the reliance on self-reported engagement measures; additionally, the paper does not provide a schema-mappable missing-data label beyond describing FIML under MCAR assumptions.
